opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a good question, because they come from pretty different traditions. MCTS as a teacher, the AlphaZero recipe, works because you have a perfect simulator. You can roll the game forward, search a few hundred or thousand nodes deep, and the search result is a strictly better policy than the raw network. Then you distill that improved policy back into the network. It's a policy improvement operator you can apply over and over.

Neural fictitious self-play, from Heinrich and Silver, is aimed at a different problem: imperfect-information games like poker. There, tree search gets awkward because you don't know the true state, only an information set. So instead of searching, NFSP keeps two networks. One is a best-response network trained with something like DQN against the opponent's current average behavior. The other is an average-policy network trained by supervised learning on your own past best responses. The average policy is what converges toward a Nash equilibrium, because fictitious play's guarantee is about the average of your strategies, not the latest one.

So I'd frame it this way: MCTS gives you a sharp local improvement signal at every state, which makes it very sample-efficient when you have a simulator and the game is deterministic and fully observed. NFSP gives you game-theoretic soundness when there's hidden information and exploitability matters, but the learning signal is much noisier. You're relying on RL to find best responses and on averaging to smooth out the cycling. In practice it's slower and less precise than search.

That's why, for poker, the strongest systems ended up combining the ideas, like ReBeL or Pluribus-style approaches that bring search back in over public belief states. To me the deeper lesson is that you want some mechanism that produces a target better than your current policy. Search does that directly. Fictitious play does it through averaging over time. If you can afford search, it's usually the stronger teacher. But if the game structure breaks the assumptions search relies on, something like NFSP is the principled fallback.

r001.rationale: The response describes MCTS improvement and NFSP strategy averaging as different mechanisms; it does not say they share a state relabeling operation.

r002.rationale: It says NFSP uses a DQN-like best-response network, but does not identify improved action labels or describe RL as replacing an MCTS teacher.

r003.rationale: It describes averaging a player’s past best responses, not distillation across possible opponents.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that the resulting mixed strategy performs no worse than an opponent selected on average from a league.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing I'd push back on a little bit is the idea that MCTS is "the teacher" in some fundamental sense. In AlphaZero the thing that actually makes it work is that you have an expensive procedure that produces a better policy than the one you currently have, and then you distill that improvement back into the network. MCTS happens to be a really good improvement operator when you have a perfect simulator and a discrete, enumerable action space. But it's not magic, it's just search amortization.

Neural fictitious self-play comes at the same problem from a game-theoretic angle. Instead of saying "let me look ahead with a tree and find a better move," you're saying "let me maintain a best response to the average of everything my opponents have done so far, and let the average strategy converge toward a Nash equilibrium." So the improvement operator there is best-response learning against a population, not lookahead. And the nice thing is you don't need a model of the environment that you can roll forward. You just need to be able to play.

Where I think that becomes attractive is in settings where the simulator is either imperfect or expensive, or where the action space isn't something you can branch over cleanly. In robotics, for example, you don't get to do a thousand rollouts from the current state. You get one shot and the physics is messy. So the MCTS-as-teacher recipe kind of falls apart, and something closer to self-play, where the curriculum comes from the other agents rather than from search, starts to look more natural.

The weakness is that fictitious self-play is slow to converge and it's really tied to the two-player zero-sum assumption. Once you move to general-sum or many-agent settings, the convergence guarantees go away and you're mostly relying on empirical luck. MCTS has the opposite problem. It converges fast but it's brittle to anything the simulator doesn't capture.

So my honest take is that I don't see them as competing teachers. I see them as two different sources of "better than you currently are" signal, and the interesting research question is how to combine them. Can you use a cheap learned best response as the thing you search over, so the tree only has to explore moves that are already plausible? Or can you use a little bit of lookahead to speed up the best-response step inside a self-play loop? That's the direction I find more exciting than picking one.

r001.rationale: The response says both methods provide an improvement signal, but it does not clearly describe their shared operation as relabeling states with better actions.

r002.rationale: It says neural fictitious self-play needs no environment model and uses best-response learning, but does not identify model-free reinforcement learning as the source of improved action labels replacing MCTS.

r003.rationale: It describes responding to the average of opponents’ past play, but does not describe mixed-strategy distillation averaging across possible opponents.

r004.rationale: The response makes no claim that the resulting mixed strategy performs no worse than an opponent selected on average from the league.

astra-6.text:
I think the appealing thing is that you can improve through interaction without having to run an expensive search procedure to produce every training target. In fictitious self-play, you train a best response to the historical mixture of your opponents’ policies, and you also learn an average policy from your own past behavior. That averaging matters: if you just train against the latest version of yourself, you can end up cycling through strategies instead of making progress.

But I wouldn’t call it a direct substitute for Monte Carlo tree search. Search gives you a way to spend additional compute on a particular decision. You take your current policy and value function, look ahead, and potentially discover a better move than the policy would have produced on its own. Then you distill that improvement back into the network. With fictitious self-play, the improvement comes from learning a best response over many interactions. You still have to solve that reinforcement learning problem.

So the question for me is where you can most effectively spend your compute. If you have a good simulator and looking ahead is tractable, search is a very powerful teacher. If you can generate lots of experience but constructing a useful search tree is difficult, self-play becomes more attractive. And the two aren’t mutually exclusive: you could use search to help produce the best responses that go into that historical mixture.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes self-play’s learning from search and distills search improvements, but does not say both methods relabel states with better actions.

r002.rationale: It identifies reinforcement learning as the source of self-play improvement, but does not specify that the learning is model-free.

r003.rationale: It describes training against a historical opponent mixture and averaging the agent’s own past behavior, but not mixed-strategy distillation by averaging across possible opponents.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that the resulting mixed strategy performs no worse than an opponent selected on average from the league.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing I find appealing about neural fictitious self-play is that your teacher is the population of policies you’ve trained so far. You learn a best response to that population, and then you fold that best response into your average strategy. So there’s this loop where reinforcement learning discovers improvements and supervised learning distills them into a policy.

With Monte Carlo tree search, you’re spending more computation at a particular position to produce a better action distribution, and then training the network to imitate that. That’s a very powerful teacher, but it depends on being able to simulate what happens next. In robotics, for example, you don’t necessarily have a simulator that’s accurate enough to search through all those possibilities.

Self-play gives you another way to generate a curriculum: as the opponent improves, the problems you have to solve become harder. And keeping the historical population matters, because otherwise you can get cycles where one policy beats another but forgets how to beat an earlier one.

I wouldn’t say it’s a replacement for search in every setting. Search gives you a mechanism for spending more compute on the specific problem in front of you. Fictitious self-play is more a mechanism for improving the training distribution and producing a robust policy over time. You could also combine the two.

r001.rationale: It says both approaches train from improved actions or distributions, but does not frame them as sharing the operation of relabeling states with better actions.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning discovers improvements, but does not identify it as model-free or describe those improvements as action labels replacing an MCTS teacher.

r003.rationale: It describes learning a best response to a population of policies and folding that response into an average strategy, communicating a mixture over possible opponents.

r004.rationale: It describes robustness and avoiding cycles, but makes no claim that the mixed strategy performs no worse than an opponent selected on average from the league.
